title: Digestion: the long tube that turns a roti into you
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 5 Biology Unit 4.1 'Parts and functions of the digestive system' (mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus, with the liver and pancreas), and goes further into enzymes, absorption, gut microbes and other animals' guts. No textbook needed.
summary: Your child follows one roti and dal from the plate to the toilet: teeth that cut and grind, saliva that turns starch into sugar, a food pipe that squeezes even when you are upside down, a stomach of acid, a small intestine as long as a room and lined with millions of tiny fingers, bile that breaks fat like soap, and a large intestine full of trillions of helpful microbes. They test saliva with iodine, squeeze a 'stomach' in a bag and an 'intestine' made of tights, and measure their own gut with a rope. Along the way they meet the fur trapper whose open stomach taught the world how digestion works, the doctor who drank bacteria to prove a point, and the cow, the rabbit and the termite, who digest what we cannot.
builds_on: This topic starts in Class 5. It builds on the Class 5 body rung (the organs and the food journey in one sentence) and the food rungs of Classes 1–4 (what food is made of, food groups and nutrients). It goes with the Class 5 food rung, which looks at a balanced diet and deficiency diseases.
subconcepts: digestion: breaking food into pieces small enough to pass into the blood
mechanical digestion: teeth, chewing and churning
chemical digestion: enzymes, and saliva turning starch into sugar
the oesophagus and peristalsis: food is squeezed, not dropped
the stomach: acid, churning, and a lining that protects itself
the small intestine: absorption through millions of villi
the liver, bile and the pancreas: helpers outside the tube
the large intestine: taking back water, fibre and faeces
gut microbes: trillions of partners that digest what we cannot
different guts for different diets: cow, rabbit, cat and termite
the gut's own nervous system and the gut–brain link
a tube through the body: inside the gut is still outside you
how we found out: experiments, credit and the people left out
ulcers, germs and who gets believed
goals: By the end your child can name, in order, the parts of the digestive system and say what each does.
By the end your child can explain the difference between mechanical and chemical digestion, with an example of each.
By the end your child can show, with iodine, that saliva breaks down starch.
By the end your child can explain how villi help absorption and why the small intestine is so long.
By the end your child can explain what gut microbes do and why a cow can live on grass but we cannot.
By the end your child can tell the stories of Alexis St Martin and of Barry Marshall and Robin Warren, and say what they show about how science works.
words: digestion
breaking food down into tiny pieces the body can absorb and use
enzyme
a substance made by the body that speeds up breaking food apart, like the amylase in saliva
saliva
the watery juice in your mouth that wets food and starts digesting starch
oesophagus
the food pipe from the throat to the stomach
peristalsis
waves of muscle squeezing that push food along the gut
stomach acid
a strong acid in the stomach that helps break down protein and kills many germs
small intestine
the long, narrow tube where most food is digested and absorbed into the blood
villi
millions of tiny finger-like bumps lining the small intestine
bile
a green juice from the liver that breaks fat into tiny drops
large intestine
the wide tube that takes water back and turns waste into faeces
fibre
the tough parts of plant food we cannot digest but our gut microbes can
microbiome
all the tiny living things, mostly bacteria, living in and on us

days.title: Where does lunch go?
days.goal: Recall what the body rung said about the food organs, draw what we think, and find out how long the gut is.

steps.title: Remember the organ map
steps.do: Ask your child: 'On the organ map in the body rung, where did food go after the mouth?' (food pipe, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, out). 'And from the food rungs, what is food made of?' (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water). Then hand them a blank body outline and ask them to draw the path of food as they imagine it, with no help. Keep the drawing: you will compare it on the last day.

steps.title: How long is your gut?
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Cut a rope or string about 7 metres long (for a child) and mark it: 25 cm for the oesophagus, a knot for the stomach, about 5 metres for the small intestine and 1.25 metres for the large intestine. Stretch it across the room or down the corridor. Ask: 'How does all this fit inside you?' (it is folded and coiled). Then stand your child next to it: 'Your gut is about four times as long as you are tall.'

steps.title: A tube through you
steps.do: Hold up a doughnut, a bangle, or a vada with a hole. Say: 'Your body is a bit like this. The gut is a tube from your mouth right through to your bottom. So, strange as it sounds, food inside your gut is not yet inside your body: it is in the hole of the doughnut. It only gets inside you when it is broken into tiny pieces small enough to pass through the gut wall into your blood. That breaking-down is called digestion.' Ask: 'So when you swallow a cherry seed and it comes out the other end, was it ever inside you?' Let them argue.

steps.title: Your body is a history book
steps.do: Say: 'The very first animals, like sponges, had no gut at all: they caught food in tiny cells. Later animals, like jellyfish and sea anemones, had a bag with one opening, a mouth that is also the exit. Then, more than 550 million years ago, scientists think, worm-like animals grew a tube with a mouth at one end and an exit at the other. That was a great invention: food could move one way, and different parts of the tube could do different jobs, like a factory line. You inherited that tube.' Ask: 'What would be the problem with a gut that has only one opening?'

need: a body outline on paper and pencils
a rope or string about 7 metres long, a marker, a measuring tape

days.title: The mouth: cutting, grinding and the first enzyme
days.goal: Find out what teeth and saliva do, and prove that saliva digests starch.

steps.title: Teeth tour
steps.do: With a mirror and clean fingers, your child finds their own teeth: flat, sharp front teeth for cutting (incisors), pointed teeth beside them for gripping and tearing (canines), and broad bumpy back teeth for grinding (molars). Bite into an apple and notice which teeth do it; chew a peanut and notice which do that. Say: 'Breaking food into smaller pieces by cutting and grinding is mechanical digestion. Smaller pieces give the digestive juices much more surface to work on.'

steps.title: The sweet bread test
steps.do: Your child chews a small piece of plain bread or a bit of plain boiled rice for two whole minutes without swallowing. Ask: 'Did the taste change?' (it gets slightly sweet). Say: 'Bread is full of starch, which is long chains of sugar stuck together. Saliva has an enzyme called amylase that cuts the chains into sugar. That is chemical digestion, and it starts in your mouth.'

steps.title: Saliva and the iodine test
steps.do: Do Experiment e1: prove it with iodine. Iodine turns blue-black when there is starch. Put a teaspoon of starchy water (water that rice or potato was boiled in, cooled) in two cups. Add a teaspoon of your child's saliva to one and a teaspoon of water to the other. Wait 10 minutes in a warm place, then add two drops of iodine to each. Ask: 'Which turned dark, and which did not? Why?'

steps.title: Enzymes: tiny scissors
steps.do: Say: 'Your body makes many enzymes, each like a pair of scissors that cuts one kind of food. Amylase cuts starch. Others in the stomach and intestine cut proteins and fats. Without enzymes, digesting a meal would take years.' Ask: 'Why did we keep the saliva cup warm?' (enzymes work best at body temperature).

need: a mirror, an apple, a few peanuts (check allergies)
two cups, starchy water from boiled rice or potato, a teaspoon, tincture of iodine or povidone-iodine (Betadine), a dropper

prep.task: Save half a cup of the water rice or potatoes were boiled in, and let it cool

days.title: Down the pipe and into the acid
days.goal: Find out how swallowing works and what the stomach does, and meet the man with a window into his stomach.

steps.title: Swallowing uphill
steps.do: Your child lies flat on a bed with the head a little lower than the feet and takes one small sip of water through a straw, and swallows (stay with them; small sips only). Ask: 'Did the water fall up into your stomach?' (no, it was pushed). Squeeze a marble or a small ball along the inside of an old sock or stocking with your hands, squeezing behind it. Say: 'Rings of muscle in the oesophagus squeeze behind the food in waves, pushing it along. This is called peristalsis. It works upside down, and it works for astronauts in space.'

steps.title: A stomach in a bag
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Put a piece of bread, a few pieces of cooked dal or banana and three tablespoons of vinegar or lemon juice (the 'acid') into a strong zip bag, squeeze the air out and close it. Your child squeezes and kneads the bag for five minutes, like the stomach's strong muscle walls. Ask: 'What does the food look like now?' (a thick soup). Say: 'A real stomach churns food for a few hours with acid strong enough to dissolve metal over time, and an enzyme that cuts protein. The soup it makes is called chyme.'

steps.title: Why doesn't the stomach digest itself?
steps.do: Ask your child to guess. Then say: 'The stomach lines itself with a thick layer of slimy mucus that the acid cannot get through, and it replaces its lining cells every few days.' Ask: 'What might happen if the mucus layer was damaged?' (the acid could make a sore, an ulcer). Say: 'Hold that thought for Day 7.'

steps.title: Read the story
steps.do: Read aloud 'The Window in My Side', the story in this rung, told by Alexis St Martin. Tell your child first that it is about a real man who was hurt and got better, and that nothing frightening is described. After reading, tell them about voice v1 and ask its question.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Start Worksheet ws1 (mouth, oesophagus and stomach sections). Finish the rest tomorrow after the intestine model.

need: a straw and a little water, an old sock and a marble or small ball
a strong zip bag, bread, cooked dal or banana, vinegar or lemon juice

days.title: The small intestine: where food gets into you
days.goal: Model absorption with tights, see why villi matter, and watch bile at work.

steps.title: Finish the core sheet
steps.do: Finish Worksheet ws1 from yesterday. Then ask: 'Our chyme soup is still in the doughnut hole. How does it get into your blood?'

steps.title: The tights intestine
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Cut one leg from an old pair of tights. Pour the stomach-bag soup from yesterday (or make a fresh one) into the tights over a bowl. Your child squeezes it along from top to bottom. Ask: 'What comes through the tights into the bowl? What stays inside?' Say: 'The liquid that passes through is like digested food passing through the wall of the small intestine into the blood. What stays inside goes on to the large intestine.'

steps.title: Towel villi
steps.do: Pour 100 ml of water onto a smooth plastic tray and 100 ml onto a small towel lying on a tray. Lift each: the smooth tray holds almost nothing; the towel soaks most of it up. Say: 'The wall of your small intestine is not smooth. It is covered in millions of tiny fingers called villi, each covered in even tinier ones. Spread out flat, the lining would cover a big room, not just a corridor. More surface means more food gets absorbed.' Ask: 'Why is a long, folded, furry tube better than a short, smooth one?'

steps.title: Bile and the oil drop
steps.do: Do Experiment e4. Put a few drops of cooking oil in a glass of water. Ask: 'Do oil and water mix?' (no, the oil floats in blobs). Add a drop of washing-up liquid and stir. The oil breaks into tiny drops. Say: 'Your liver makes bile, a green juice stored in a little bag called the gall bladder. Bile does to fat what the soap did to the oil: breaks it into tiny drops so enzymes from the pancreas can cut them. The pancreas, a long gland behind the stomach, pours enzymes for starch, protein and fat into the small intestine too.'

need: the bag of stomach soup, or bread, banana and vinegar to make more
an old pair of tights, scissors, a bowl
a smooth tray, a small towel, a measuring jug
a glass, cooking oil, washing-up liquid, a spoon

days.title: The large intestine and our trillions of partners
days.goal: Find out what happens to what is left, and meet the microbes that live in our gut.

steps.title: What's left?
steps.do: Look at what stayed inside the tights yesterday (or think about it). Ask: 'What is left after the small intestine has taken the food?' (water, fibre from plants, old cells, bacteria). Say: 'The large intestine is wider and shorter. It takes back most of the water, so we do not dry out, and it shapes what is left into faeces, which wait in the rectum until we go to the toilet. If too little water is taken back, we get diarrhoea; if too much, we get constipation.' Ask: 'Why do doctors tell people to eat fibre and drink water?'

steps.title: The microbes in you
steps.do: Say: 'In your large intestine live trillions of bacteria and other microbes, hundreds of different kinds. The best count, from 2016, says there are about as many bacteria in you as there are human cells. They eat the fibre we cannot digest, and in return make vitamins and substances that feed the cells of your gut wall and help train your body's defences. They are not invaders. They are partners.' Show a bowl of dahi: 'Dahi is milk changed by helpful bacteria. Idli batter, dosa batter, kanji and pickles are made by microbes too.'

steps.title: You are One and Many
steps.do: Do Activity a2, the journal page 'You are One and Many'. On the left your child draws themselves as one person. On the right they draw a 'zoom' into the large intestine, crowded with different shaped microbes (rods, balls, spirals, chains), and label three things the microbes do: eat fibre, make vitamins, crowd out harmful germs. Ask: 'If about half of the living cells in and on you are not human, who is "you"?' Listen; there is no right answer.

steps.title: Do gut microbes affect how we feel?
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v4, the debate over whether gut microbes affect mood and behaviour. Also say: 'Your gut has its own network of hundreds of millions of nerve cells, sometimes called the "second brain". It runs digestion by itself and sends messages to the brain. That is one reason you feel "butterflies" when nervous.' Ask the voice question.

need: paper and coloured pencils for the journal page

days.title: Different guts for different lives
days.goal: Compare how a cow, a rabbit, a cat and a termite digest, and weigh the appendix debate.

steps.title: Grass-eaters and meat-eaters
steps.do: Say: 'Grass and leaves are full of cellulose, a tough fibre that no animal can digest by itself. So plant-eaters keep armies of microbes to do it.' The cow: a stomach with four chambers; the biggest, the rumen, is a giant vat of microbes digesting grass; the cow brings food back up and chews it again (chewing the cud). The rabbit: a big pouch called the caecum full of microbes, and it eats some of its own soft droppings to digest the food a second time. The cat: a meat-eater with a short, simple gut, because meat is easy to digest. The termite: eats wood, and the microbes in its gut digest it. Ask: 'Which animals are really doing the digesting, the cow or its microbes?' (both, together).

steps.title: Drama: the journey of a roti
steps.do: Do Activity a3. Each family member (or toy) is a part: Mouth, Oesophagus, Stomach, Small Intestine, Liver, Large Intestine, Microbes. A ball of paper is the roti. Pass it along; each part says its line and does its action (Mouth: 'Cut and grind, and here's some saliva!'; Oesophagus: squeeze; Stomach: churn and pour acid; Liver: squirt bile; Small Intestine: tear off little bits of paper and 'absorb' them into a box marked BLOOD; Microbes: nibble the 'fibre'; Large Intestine: squeeze out the water). End at a bin marked EXIT.

steps.title: The appendix debate
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v3, the appendix. Ask the voice question and ask your child which side they lean to, and why.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 together on the intestines, microbes and other animals' guts.

need: a ball of paper, small paper scraps, a box marked BLOOD, a bin marked EXIT

days.title: Who gets believed?
days.goal: Hear how ulcers were found to be caused by a germ, and start building a model digestive system.

steps.title: The doctor who drank bacteria
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v2, Barry Marshall and Robin Warren. Ask: 'For years doctors said ulcers came from stress and spicy food. Why do you think they found it so hard to believe a germ could live in stomach acid?' Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: The Long Tube board game
steps.do: Play the board game g1, from MOUTH to EXIT. Each square is a part of the gut or a helper; say what happens there as you land.

steps.title: Start the project
steps.do: Start the project: build a model of the whole digestive system from things at home. Choose a material for each part that matches its job: a funnel or cup for the mouth, a long straw or pipe for the oesophagus, a balloon or zip bag for the stomach, a long coiled tube or tights for the small intestine, a wider tube (a toilet-roll chain) for the large intestine, a sponge for the liver. Glue or tape them onto a big card in the right places and order. Today: plan and gather; finish tomorrow.

need: the printed board game, a die and counters
funnel, straws or pipe, a balloon or bag, tights or tubing, toilet rolls, a sponge, tape, glue and a big card

days.title: Teach it back
days.goal: Finish the model, compare with the first drawing, do the challenge sheet and teach it back.

steps.title: Finish and compare
steps.do: Finish the model from yesterday and label every part with its job. Then put the first-day drawing next to it. Ask: 'What did you get right on Day 1? What has changed?' Write three things they now know that they did not before.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. These ask for reasons; let your child argue.

steps.title: Big question
steps.do: Ask: 'The roti you ate yesterday is now part of your blood and your muscles, and some of it fed your microbes. Where does food end and you begin?'

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child uses the model to teach a grown-up the whole journey: what each part does, mechanical and chemical digestion, absorption, the microbes, and one story of how it was found out. Then ask the check questions.

sections.p: Which is the right order?
opts: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, anus
mouth, stomach, oesophagus, large intestine, small intestine, anus
mouth, small intestine, stomach, oesophagus, anus

sections.p: Match each part to its job.
pairs: wets food and starts digesting starch
squeezes food down to the stomach
absorbs digested food into the blood

opts: stayed lighter because the starch was broken down

sections.p: Why did the bread taste sweeter after two minutes of chewing?
Why doesn't the stomach digest itself?

sections.p: Bile from the liver…

Match the animal to its digestion.

a short gut for easy-to-digest meat

opts: its gut microbes digest cellulose for it

sections.p: Who digests it first: us, or our gut microbes?
Your food is not 'inside' you until it passes through the gut wall. Explain what that means using the doughnut idea.
Why might taking antibiotics sometimes upset your tummy? Use the word microbes.
Beaumont put stomach juice and meat in a warm bottle. The meat dissolved. What did that show?

items: a germ causes most stomach ulcers

sections.p: The famous self-experimenter who drank Helicobacter pylori was Barry ____.
Alexis St Martin's body taught the world about digestion, but William Beaumont's name is the one on the book. Who deserves the credit, and how should we remember St Martin?
Barry Marshall drank bacteria to test his idea on himself. Was that brave, foolish, or both? Should scientists ever test on themselves?
About half the living cells in and on you are microbes, and they help digest your food. Are they part of you? Give reasons for yes and for no.

experiments.title: Saliva and the iodine test
experiments.question: Does saliva digest starch?
need: half a cup of cooled starchy water (from boiling rice or potato)
tincture of iodine or povidone-iodine (Betadine), and a dropper
steps: First test: put a drop of iodine on a piece of bread or potato on a white plate. It turns blue-black: that shows starch.
Put two teaspoons of starchy water in each cup.
Your child spits about a teaspoon of saliva into cup A. Add a teaspoon of plain water to cup B. Label them.
Stir and leave both somewhere warm (in a bowl of warm water) for 10–15 minutes.
Add two drops of iodine to each cup and compare the colour.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which cup will turn blue-black? Will the saliva make a difference?'
experiments.observe: Cup B (water) turns dark blue-black. Cup A (saliva) stays lighter, brown or yellow, because much of the starch has gone.
experiments.why: Iodine sticks to the long coiled chains of starch and turns blue-black. Saliva contains the enzyme amylase, which cuts starch chains into smaller sugars that iodine does not colour. Warmth helps because enzymes work best near body temperature. Cup B is the control: everything the same except the saliva, so the saliva must be what made the difference.
experiments.safety: Iodine is poisonous if swallowed and stains skin and clothes. An adult handles it, and nothing from the cups is tasted. Wash hands afterwards. Do not use iodine if anyone at home has an iodine allergy.

experiments.title: A stomach in a bag
experiments.question: What does the stomach do to food?
need: a small banana or cooked dal
three tablespoons of vinegar or lemon juice
steps: Tear the bread and break the banana into the bag.
Add the vinegar or lemon juice and a splash of water.
Squeeze out the air and seal it well.
Your child kneads and squeezes the bag for five minutes.
Look at and describe the mixture. Keep it for tomorrow's experiment.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will the food look like after five minutes of squeezing in acid?'
experiments.observe: The food breaks down into a lumpy, then smoother, soup.
experiments.why: The stomach's thick muscle walls squeeze and churn food for a few hours (mechanical digestion), while hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin start breaking proteins apart (chemical digestion). The acid also kills many germs swallowed with food. Vinegar and lemon juice are much weaker acids than stomach acid, so the model shows the idea, not the strength.
experiments.safety: Use a strong bag and check the seal. Do not eat the mixture.

experiments.title: The tights intestine
experiments.question: How does digested food get out of the gut and into the blood?
need: one leg cut from an old pair of tights
steps: Hold the tights leg over the bowl.
Pour the soup into the open end.
Your child squeezes from the top down, slowly, like peristalsis.
Watch what drips into the bowl.
At the end, cut open the foot and look at what is left inside.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will get through the tights, and what will stay inside?'
experiments.observe: Liquid with tiny particles passes through into the bowl; lumps and fibres stay inside.
experiments.why: In the small intestine, food is digested into molecules small enough to pass through the gut wall into the blood, which carries them to every cell. The liquid in the bowl is like absorbed food. What stays behind, like fibre, goes on to the large intestine. Real absorption is much more selective than a filter: the gut wall cells actively take up sugars and other nutrients.
experiments.safety: Wash hands after. Do not eat the mixture.

experiments.title: Bile and the oil drop
experiments.question: How does the body digest fat, which does not mix with water?
steps: Pour a teaspoon of oil into the water. Stir and watch.
Leave it for a minute: the oil floats back up in blobs.
Add one drop of washing-up liquid and stir again.
Compare how the oil looks now.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Can we make the oil mix into the water?'
experiments.observe: Without soap, oil makes big blobs that float. With soap, it breaks into many tiny drops that stay in the water and make it cloudy.
experiments.why: Fat does not mix with water, so enzymes in the watery gut can only reach the outside of big fat blobs. Bile from the liver acts like soap: it breaks fat into tiny drops (emulsifies it), giving the fat-cutting enzymes from the pancreas much more surface to work on. This is mechanical help for chemical digestion.
experiments.safety: Do not drink the water. Washing-up liquid stings eyes.

activities.title: How long is your gut?
need: a rope or string about 7 metres long
steps: Measure and mark: 25 cm for the oesophagus.
Tie a big knot for the stomach.
Measure about 5 metres for the small intestine and mark its end.
Measure about 1.25 metres for the large intestine.
Lay it straight across the floor or a corridor, then coil it up into a space the size of your child's belly.
activities.outcome: A feel for how long the gut is (about four times your child's height) and how much folding it takes to fit inside.

activities.title: You are One and Many (journal page)
steps: On the left half, draw yourself whole: the One.
On the right half, draw a big circle as if zooming into the large intestine.
Fill it with microbes of many shapes: rods, balls, spirals, chains.
Label three jobs they do for you.
Write underneath: 'I am one, and I am many.'
activities.outcome: A journal page showing your child as one person and as a community of trillions of living things.

activities.title: Drama: the journey of a roti
need: a ball of paper as the roti
steps: Give each person or toy a role: Mouth, Oesophagus, Stomach, Liver, Pancreas, Small Intestine, Microbes, Large Intestine.
Each makes up one line and one action for their job.
Pass the roti along the line, each doing their action.
The Small Intestine tears off pieces and puts them in BLOOD.
The Large Intestine squeezes out 'water' and drops what is left in EXIT.
Swap roles and play again faster.
activities.outcome: A short family play of the digestive system, with every part's job acted out.

project.title: Build a model digestive system
steps: List each part of the digestive system and its job.
Choose a material for each part that matches its shape and job (a balloon stretches like a stomach; tights let liquid through like the intestine wall).
Fix the parts onto a big card in the right order and place, with the liver and pancreas beside the tube.
Label each part and its job.
Write two ways your model is like the real system and two ways it is not.
Use it to teach someone.
project.outcome: A labelled model digestive system made from waste materials, with an honest comparison to the real thing.

game.title: The Long Tube
rules: You are a mouthful of roti and dal. Start at MOUTH.
Roll and move along the tube.
On each square, say what happens to you there before you can roll again next turn.
Absorption squares let you 'get into the body': collect a token for each.
The first to reach EXIT wins, but the player with most absorption tokens gets a bonus round.
squares: STOMACH: churned in acid, miss a turn
Acid kills a germ riding on you: +1
Bile from the liver breaks your fat
Villi absorb your sugar: take a token
Absorbed into the blood: take a token
Absorbed amino acids: take a token
Microbes make a vitamin: take a token
Not enough water today: constipation, miss a turn

big: The roti you ate is now part of your blood and muscle. Where does food end and you begin?
About half the living cells in and on you are microbes. Who is 'you'?
A cow cannot digest grass without its microbes. Who is really the grass-eater?
If food in your gut is still 'outside' you, is anything really inside you?
Alexis St Martin's body taught the world about digestion. Who owns what we learn from a person's body?

challenge.q: Spicy food and stress cause stomach ulcers.
challenge.hint: For decades doctors thought so. Robin Warren and Barry Marshall showed that most stomach ulcers are caused by a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, and can be cured with antibiotics; they won the Nobel Prize in 2005. Some ulcers are caused by painkiller medicines like aspirin. Chilli does not cause ulcers. Ask: why do you think the old idea lasted so long?

challenge.q: Swallowed chewing gum stays in your stomach for seven years.
challenge.hint: Not true. The gum base cannot be digested, but peristalsis moves it along like any other undigested thing, and it leaves the body in a few days. (Swallowing lots at once is still a bad idea for small children.) Ask: how could a doctor know?

challenge.q: Bacteria are germs, and germs are bad.
challenge.hint: A few kinds of bacteria cause disease. Most of the trillions in your gut are helpful partners that digest fibre, make vitamins and crowd out harmful ones. Dahi, idli and dosa batter are made by bacteria. Ask: is it fair to judge a whole kingdom of life by its worst members?

challenge.q: The stomach does most of the digesting.
challenge.hint: The stomach churns and starts digesting proteins, but most digestion and nearly all absorption happens in the small intestine, with help from the liver and pancreas. People can even live without most of their stomach. Ask: why do you think people imagine the stomach is the main part?

perspectives.view: To a cow, grass is a feast because of the microbes she carries in her rumen. Without them she would starve in a green field. Ask: is a cow one animal, or a team?

Ayurveda speaks of 'agni', the digestive fire, and teaches eating at regular times, eating warm, freshly cooked food and not eating too much at once. Some of these habits fit modern advice; the idea of agni is a way of describing digestion, not a thing a scientist can measure. Ask: can an old way of describing something still give good advice?
What leaves our bodies is food for dung beetles, fungi and soil bacteria, who turn it back into soil that grows plants. Ask: is there really such a thing as 'waste' in nature?

perspectives.who: A family who makes idli batter overnight
perspectives.view: Every night across South India, rice and urad dal batter rises in warm kitchens because wild bacteria and yeasts eat its sugars and make gas. Ask: who is really cooking: the family, or the microbes?

voices.who: Alexis St Martin (about 1794–1880), a French-Canadian fur trader, and William Beaumont (1785–1853), a US army surgeon
voices.idea: In June 1822, on Mackinac Island in North America, a gun went off by accident and wounded the young fur trader Alexis St Martin in the side. The army surgeon William Beaumont saved his life, but the wound healed leaving a small opening into his stomach. Over about ten years Beaumont did experiments through it: lowering food on a silk thread and pulling it out to see how much was digested, and taking out stomach juice and showing that it digested meat in a warm bottle outside the body. He published a famous book in 1833.
voices.then: Before this many people thought the stomach mostly ground or cooked food. Beaumont showed that digestion was chemical, done by an acid juice. He became famous as the 'father of gastric physiology'.
voices.now: Historians now also ask about St Martin. He was poor and could not read; he signed contracts to work as Beaumont's servant so the experiments could go on, sometimes ran away, and was often unwell from them. He outlived Beaumont by 27 years. When he died, his family let his body be buried very deep so that no doctor could take it.
voices.ask: The knowledge came from St Martin's body, and the fame went to Beaumont. Was the arrangement fair? What would have made it fairer?

voices.who: Robin Warren (1937–2024) and Barry Marshall (born 1951), Perth, Australia
voices.idea: In the early 1980s the pathologist Robin Warren kept seeing curved bacteria in samples from inflamed stomachs. With the young doctor Barry Marshall, he proposed that this bacterium, later called Helicobacter pylori, causes stomach ulcers. Nearly everyone believed ulcers came from stress, spicy food and too much acid, and that no bacterium could live in stomach acid.
voices.then: Their idea was laughed at. When tests on animals did not work, in 1984 Marshall, then 32, drank a culture of the bacteria himself. He became ill with stomach inflammation, a test showed the bacteria had taken hold, and he treated himself with antibiotics.
voices.now: After many careful trials, ulcers are now cured with antibiotics instead of years of medicines or surgery. Warren and Marshall won the Nobel Prize in 2005. Self-experiments like Marshall's are now discouraged: modern research must pass ethics checks to protect volunteers.
voices.ask: Marshall was so sure he tested it on himself. Is being very sure enough to make you right? What else did they need?

voices.who: The appendix debate: Charles Darwin (1871) and William Parker, Heather Smith and colleagues (2007 onwards)
voices.idea: Darwin suggested that the human appendix, a small pouch off the start of the large intestine, is a shrunken leftover of a bigger pouch our plant-eating ancestors used to digest leaves, now useless. Parker and colleagues argued in 2007 that it is a 'safe house' for helpful gut bacteria, which can regrow the gut's microbes after a bad bout of diarrhoea. Smith and colleagues found the appendix has evolved independently in many mammals, more than 30 times, which suggests it is useful.
voices.then: For over a century the appendix was taught as the textbook example of a useless organ.
voices.now: Many scientists now think it has a job in the immune system and as a bacteria store, but it is still debated how important that job is. People who have their appendix removed live normal, healthy lives.
voices.ask: If people live well without an appendix, can it still be useful? What evidence would settle the question?

voices.who: John Cryan, Ted Dinan and other gut–brain researchers (Ireland and elsewhere), and their critics
voices.idea: From the 2000s, experiments showed that mice raised with no gut microbes at all behave differently from normal mice, and that moving gut microbes from one mouse to another can change some behaviours. Cryan and Dinan's team and others suggested that gut microbes may affect mood and stress in people too, through nerves, hormones and the immune system.
voices.then: The idea excited scientists and the public, and many companies began selling 'probiotic' products with big promises.
voices.now: That gut and brain talk to each other is well accepted. How much gut microbes change human mood is still uncertain: most strong results are in mice, human studies are small and mixed, and many product claims go far beyond the evidence.
voices.ask: A result in mice is exciting. What would you need to see before you believed it was true for children?

books.title: What Happens to a Hamburger?
books.author: Paul Showers
books.why: A clear, friendly classic that follows food from the mouth to the intestines, with simple home tests.

books.title: Gut: The Inside Story of Our Body's Most Underrated Organ
books.author: Giulia Enders
books.why: A funny, warm and accurate book by a young German doctor about digestion and gut microbes, with cartoons by her sister Jill.

books.title: Gajapati Kulapati
books.author: Ashok Rajagopalan
books.why: A big elephant eats too many coconuts and gets a terrible tummy ache: a funny Indian picture book for talking about what happens in the gut.

books.title: The Way We Work
books.author: David Macaulay
books.why: The digestion chapter has superb cut-away drawings of teeth, stomach, villi and intestines.

check.q: Name the parts of the digestive system in order.
check.a: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, anus; with the liver, gall bladder and pancreas as helpers.

check.q: What is the difference between mechanical and chemical digestion? Give an example of each.
check.a: Mechanical breaks food into smaller pieces (chewing, churning); chemical breaks it into different, smaller substances with enzymes and acid (amylase turning starch into sugar).

check.q: What did the iodine test show?
check.a: Starch with saliva stayed light because amylase broke the starch down; starch with water turned blue-black.

check.q: Why is the small intestine long and covered in villi?
check.a: To give a huge surface area so digested food can be absorbed into the blood.

check.q: What do the large intestine and its microbes do?
check.a: The large intestine takes back water and forms faeces; microbes digest fibre, make vitamins and help keep us healthy.

check.q: How does a cow digest grass?
check.a: Microbes in its rumen digest the cellulose; it chews the cud to break it down more.

check.q: What did Alexis St Martin's stomach teach Beaumont?
check.a: That digestion is chemical: stomach juice digested food even outside the body.

story.title: The Window in My Side
text: My name is Alexis St Martin. I was born in Canada, near Montreal, and I cannot read or write, so I am telling you this out loud. I am an old man now, and I have been famous for most of my life, though hardly anybody knows my face. What they know is my stomach.

When I was young I was a voyageur. I paddled great canoes loaded with furs across the lakes and rivers of the north, singing to keep the rhythm, for the American Fur Company. In the summer of 1822 I was at the trading post on Mackinac Island, in the middle of the great lakes, with all the other paddlers and trappers. The store was crowded. Somebody's gun went off by accident. It went into my side.

I will not tell you about that part. I was asleep for most of it, I think. What matters is that an army doctor called William Beaumont came running from the fort, and he looked at me and said I would not live through the day. He was wrong. I was young and strong, and he was a good doctor, and he cleaned the wound and dressed it every day for many months, and slowly I got better.

But the wound did not close all the way. It left a little opening in my side, about as wide as a finger, that went right into my stomach. Over time a soft fold of skin grew over it, like a little door, so that my dinner stayed inside. If you pressed on the fold, the door opened, and you could look straight into me.
The doctor could look into me. He was the first person in the world who had ever been able to watch, day after day, what a living stomach does.
And so I became his experiment.

He would tie bits of food to a silk thread: a piece of beef, a piece of raw cabbage, a lump of bread, salted pork. He would push them gently through my little door into my stomach, and then, every hour, he would pull the thread out and look at what was left. The bread went quickly. The cabbage took longer. The fat pork took longest of all. He wrote it all down in his notebook in neat lines. I lay on the bed and watched him write things I could not read about a body that was mine.

I did not always like it. Sometimes it made my stomach sore, and sometimes I was tired of being poked and timed, and once I ran away home to Canada for four years and married and had children. But I was poor, and the doctor paid me, and in the end I signed a paper, with a cross because I cannot write my name, saying I would be his servant so that he could go on.
I want to tell you about the day he understood.

In those days the wise doctors argued about what the stomach really did. Some said it ground food up, like a mill. Some said it cooked food, with its warmth. Some said it made food rot. Nobody knew, because nobody had ever watched.

One morning the doctor put a little rubber tube through my door and let some of the clear juice from my empty stomach run out into a small glass bottle. It was sour, he said, sour like vinegar, and a little sticky. Then he took a piece of boiled beef, cut it small, and dropped it into the bottle of my juice. He closed it and kept it warm, as warm as the inside of a man. He put another piece of beef into a bottle of plain water, kept it warm the same way, as a comparison.
Then we waited.

Over the hours, the beef in the water just sat there, getting soft. But the beef in my juice began to change. Its edges went fuzzy. It broke into threads. Then the threads broke. By the next day there was hardly any beef left at all: only a cloudy soup.

The doctor held the bottle up to the window, and his hand was shaking. My stomach was not in the bottle. Nothing was grinding. Nothing was churning. It was only the juice, alone, outside of any body, and still it was eating the meat.
“It is the juice,” he said. “Alexis, it is a chemical. Digestion is a chemical.”

I looked at the bottle of cloudy soup, and then down at my side, at the little door, and I thought: so that is what has been going on in there, all my life, without my knowing. A sour juice, quietly turning beef into me.
The doctor wrote a famous book. It has his name on it. Doctors in many countries read it, and he became known as the father of something with a long name. In the book I am 'the subject'.

I have lived a long time since. I went back to Canada and worked as a farmer and a woodcutter and raised my family. Doctors still write to me, asking me to come and be looked at, offering money. Once one of them asked whether, after I die, he could have my stomach for his museum.

I have told my children what to do. When I die, they are to keep me at home in the warm for a few days, and then dig my grave very deep, deeper than any doctor will dig. I have lent my stomach to the world for long enough.
It was a fine thing, what we found out, the doctor and I. But it was my side the window was in.
story.epiphany: Digestion is chemical as well as mechanical: stomach juice digests meat even in a warm bottle outside the body, while the control bottle of water does not. The turn is the cloudy bottle held up to the window. Underneath, gently: the knowledge came from a poor, unlettered man's body, and the fame went to the man who wrote the book.
ask: What did the doctor learn from the food on the silk thread?
Why did he put a second piece of beef in plain water?
What did the bottle of stomach juice show that surprised him?
How did Alexis feel about being 'the subject'? How do you know?
Why did Alexis want his grave dug so deep?

ideas.idea: You are a tube, and food is outside you until it is digested.
ideas.more: The gut runs from mouth to anus like the hole in a doughnut. Food enters your body only when it is broken into molecules small enough to pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood.

Enzymes in saliva, stomach, pancreas and intestine cut food into its building blocks; the liver's bile breaks up fat; and trillions of gut microbes digest the fibre we cannot. A cow eating grass is really a cow and her microbes eating grass together.

ideas.idea: Your gut is a history book.
ideas.more: The one-way gut tube was invented by worm-like animals over 550 million years ago, and plant-eaters everywhere solved cellulose the same way: by partnering with microbes.

unknowns: How much do gut microbes affect our mood, thinking and health? Scientists are just beginning to find out, and many claims go beyond the evidence.
What is the appendix really for, and how much does it matter? Still debated.
Why do some people's guts react badly to foods that others digest easily? Scientists understand some cases, like lactose intolerance, but not many others.
